name: Tara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this, Tara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union or party, and your name won't be attached to anything. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Days, I do prescription deliveries for three pharmacies through a delivery app, in my own hatchback, mostly to older people on the edge of town. Evenings, three nights a week, I do takeaway orders on a food app. I like the pharmacy runs because people are glad to see me, and Mrs Okafor on Birch Close always has the kettle on. What wears me out is the evening shift on a Friday when the app keeps stacking two orders going opposite ways.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And the money and home side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Together it adds up to normal pay for a driver round here. I share a flat with my older sister Selin, she works in a bank call centre. I've got about three months of savings, which I started after my car failed its safety test last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so basically today, carried on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected, there's a lot of noise about AI. I'd probably share a funny post about it. Nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the pharmacy work is pretty steady, older people need their medicine whatever happens. The food app is the shaky part, the pay per order has dropped twice in two years. And my car is nine years old, so that's always in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both jobs as they are. I'd keep putting 40 a week towards a newer car, because the old one won't last forever. I might drop one evening shift if the food pay drops again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit flat. Like most weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the food pay dropped twice. How much did that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe 25 or 30 a week in total. It doesn't sound like much, but that's my car insurance. I notice it every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Selin's job in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even with AI as hype, the bank is putting in chat bots for simple questions, and my sister's team didn't replace two people who left. So even in the boring version, we've got one job in the house that's slowly shrinking.

say: That's what I **expected**; there's a lot of noise about AI.
I'd share a **funny post** about it, nothing serious.
think: The **pharmacy runs** are steady because people always need their medicine.
The **food app** pay has dropped twice in two years, and my car is nine years old.
do: Keep **both jobs**, pharmacy days and three food evenings.
Save **40 a week** towards a newer car.
Drop an **evening shift** if food pay falls again.
feel: **Okay** and a bit **flat**, like most weeks.
S0.quote: Even with AI as hype, the bank is putting in chat bots for simple questions, and my sister's team didn't replace two people who left.
fieldNote: Her **pharmacy work** feels secure; the food app is the shaky part.
Her sister's **call centre job** is already shrinking, even in a no-change world.
Pre-existing pressures: an **old car** and falling food-app pay.

steps.text: Keep pharmacy deliveries by day and three food-app evenings
Save 40 a week towards replacing the nine-year-old hatchback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what's starting to happen at Selin's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to keep an eye on it and learn a bit. I'm not against AI, I use the chat thing now and then to write a complaint to the app. I'd say most people will be fine if they're sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my driving is mostly safe for a while, because the robots come slowly. But my sister answers customers for a bank, and that's exactly the list on your card. If she loses her job, our rent is on me, and I can't do it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the pharmacy manager, Mr Patel, whether they'd train me as a pharmacy assistant on the counter, part-time. I'd keep driving the rest. And I'd sit down with Selin and work out a plan if her job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More for Selin than for me, and that's not a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the pharmacy counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know the medicines by name from the bags I carry, and I know the regulars. It's people work. And Mr Patel has said before that I'd be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Selin's job went, what's the first thing you'd change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look for a smaller flat, or take in a lodger in the box room. I'd do an extra evening shift. And I'd make her apply everywhere, she's slow to start things.

say: It's sensible to **keep an eye** on AI and learn a bit.
Most people will be **fine** if they're sensible.
think: My driving is mostly safe for now because **robots come slowly**.
My sister answers customers for a bank, and if her job goes the **rent is on me**.
do: Ask the pharmacy manager about **counter training** as a part-time assistant.
Keep **driving** the rest of the week.
Make a **household plan** with Selin in case her job goes.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for her sister than for herself.
S1.quote: My sister answers customers for a bank, and that's exactly the list on your card.
fieldNote: She separates her **hands-on job** from her sister's exposed **desk job**.
Her risk runs through **shared rent**, not her own work.
The pharmacy counter is a **natural next step** built on known relationships.

steps.text: Ask Mr Patel about part-time counter training at the pharmacy
Keep pharmacy deliveries and food evenings going
Plan with Selin for a lodger or smaller flat if her job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs to slow it down or help people, one or the other. I'd say both companies and politicians dropped the ball. I wouldn't post much, I'd talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the bank's call centre would be gone by 2028, so Selin's out first. Then around 2031 the robots can do my driving and carrying. Even the pharmacy counter is partly checking prescriptions, which is thinking work, so that changes in 2028 too. I'd be 31, with both of us out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the pharmacy counter training straight away, focusing on the people side, because the checking side goes to AI. I'd cut everything to save six months. I'd ask our parents about moving back in with them if it got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night with the spreadsheet. Two incomes going in five years is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving back with your parents. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like failing, honestly, even though it's sensible. They're forty minutes away on the bus. My mum would love it and I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mrs Okafor and the other regulars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'll keep coming as long as the app sends me. Some of them don't have anyone else who visits. I don't think a robot will bring the milk in for them.

say: This is **too fast**: the government should slow it or help people.
Both **companies and politicians** dropped the ball.
think: The bank's call centre goes by 2028, so **Selin's out first**.
Even the counter is partly **checking prescriptions**, which AI would take in 2028 too.
do: Start **counter training** at once, focusing on the people side.
Ask our parents about **moving back** if it gets bad.
feel: **Alarmed**, up at night with the spreadsheet over two incomes going.
S2.quote: Even the pharmacy counter is partly checking prescriptions, which is thinking work, so that changes in 2028 too.
fieldNote: She spots that the **pharmacy counter** has a thinking side that goes first.
Both household earners at risk drives her **alarm**.
Moving home to her **parents** feels like failure to her, though sensible.

steps.text: Start pharmacy counter training now, focusing on patient-facing work
Build savings to six months of expenses
Cut takeaways, streaming and the gym membership
Ask her parents about moving back in if both jobs go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives you a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people start now, so there's no reason to panic. I'd say it to Selin first. I'd say the government should pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still worry about Selin, but she'd have time to move. For me, the driving lasts until about 2034, and I can learn something in seven years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Patel about counter training in the first year and keep driving. I'd help Selin look for a new job before the call centre closes. I'd keep saving 40 a week and maybe bump it to 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more manageable. Like a long hill instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Selin look for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something with people face to face, like the council's housing office or a care job. She's good on the phone, so maybe something where you meet people. I'd make her do the applications on Sunday nights with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave driving earlier than you have to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the counter job paid the same, yes. I like the pharmacy runs, but I don't love the Friday nights. I'd drop the food app first.

say: Five years is **enough time** if people start now, so there's no reason to panic.
think: My driving lasts until about **2034**, which is seven years to learn something.
My sister would have **time to move** before the call centre closes.
do: Ask about **counter training** in the first year while driving.
Raise savings from **40 to 60** a week.
feel: **Anxious but manageable**, like a long hill instead of a cliff.
S3.quote: For me, the driving lasts until about 2034, and I can learn something in seven years.
fieldNote: Five years lowers her mood but the **household risk** keeps her anxious.
She'd **drop the food app** first, keeping the pharmacy runs she likes.
She takes charge of her sister's **job search**.

steps.text: Ask about pharmacy counter training in the first year
Raise savings from 40 to 60 a week
Help Selin apply for face-to-face jobs on Sunday nights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Plenty of time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's plan properly. Online I'd probably share something practical, like where to find courses. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine for a long while. The driving goes around 2039, when I'm 40. Selin's job goes around 2036, so she's got time too. It's the slow version I can actually picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the counter training in the next couple of years, part-time. I'd keep driving the pharmacy runs and drop the food evenings. I'd keep saving and maybe help Selin pick a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's a worry for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own plans, like moving or relationships?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like my own place by 30, with or without a partner, and ten years makes that feel possible. Two years would have killed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently if you were sure it was ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably buy a newer car and stick with the pharmacy work longer. It's the sure thing that changes the plan. But nobody's ever sure.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, so let's plan properly.
I'd share **practical tips** online, like where to find courses.
think: The driving goes around **2039**, when I'm 40.
My sister's job goes around **2036**, so she has time too.
do: Do **counter training** part-time within a couple of years.
Keep the **pharmacy runs** and drop food evenings.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly fine, a worry for later.
S4.quote: I'd like my own place by 30, with or without a partner, and ten years makes that feel possible.
fieldNote: The decade lets her picture **owning a home**, which shorter timelines rule out.
She stays **practical** and calm in public and private.
Her plan narrows to the **pharmacy work** she likes most.

steps.text: Do part-time pharmacy counter training within two years
Keep pharmacy deliveries and drop food-app evenings
Save towards her own flat by age 30

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my sister and I would both lose work within a few years of each other and we share the rent. What would help is paid training in people jobs, like pharmacy counter work, and some help with rent while you change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the older people. Some of the older people I deliver medicine to only see me all week. I'd want whoever designs the robots to remember that.

headlineQuote: Some of the older people I deliver medicine to only see me all week.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old driver** who does pharmacy deliveries by day and food orders three nights a week.
She shares a flat with her **sister Selin**, a bank call centre worker whose job is more exposed than hers.
She is **practical and steady**, and her plan is to train for the pharmacy counter.
Her worry runs through the **shared rent**: two incomes at risk in the fast AGI picture.
She values the **human side** of her rounds, especially lonely older customers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when both she and her sister would lose work within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** for people jobs like pharmacy counter work.
